sentences.sentence: It flew by quicker than I could comprehend.
The only thing I could see was the same bored face that the man had.
It was the saddest thing I'd ever seen in my life so far.
The common factor in this man's entire life was a small, old-fashioned mechanical watch that he wore.
It was something I had seen before, many times before, but this time it held a different significance.
There was a small button on the side, a small black button, and it looked so out of place on that elegant time piece.
He looked at me with a mixture of frustration and annoyance.
He looked at me, then at the watch, and his face changed for a second.
A small light sparkled in his eyes and he smiled.
'Yes I do,' he said.
He turned it over to the side, and I saw the small black button.
He looked at me with the sad face again, and said, 'Let me show you.'
He pressed the button, and the room around us started to change.
We went back, a lot farther back, to a time when he was a young man.
He was a young man with a lot of hope in his eyes.
He was sitting in a small room, with a lot of nice things around him, but he was still sad.
He looked at the watch and said, 'This is what brought me here.'
I looked at the watch and I looked at the room.
He said, 'It lets me experience a life, in a few minutes.'
A life in a few minutes?
What did he mean?
The words on the page tremble slightly as I try and read.
I stare at the scribbled handwriting, trying to make sense of it, but the name at the top of the page is one that brings back a flood of memories, memories I thought were long buried.
It's my brother's handwriting, my brother who died 17 years ago in a tragic accident on our family's trip to the lake house.

I feel like I'm reading a letter from the dead, and it's not just the words that make me feel that way - it's the weight of this package in my hands, the weight of possibility that he might have actually sent it.
I look around my apartment, trying to get my bearings, but everything feels different now.
The TV, the couch, the bookshelf - it's all still here, but nothing feels the same.
I take the letter off the top of the package and look at it closer, my mind trying to make sense of how this is possible.
It's my brother's handwriting, no doubt about it, but it's like he wrote it yesterday, not 17 years ago.
I try and shake my head, to clear it, to wake up, but I'm awake.
This is my reality.
I try to open the package, but my hands are shaking too much.
I set it down on the table and try to get my head around this.
My brother is dead.
He died in an accident on our lake house, a slip on the dock and a fall into the water.
We were on summer vacation, just the two of us, and it happened.
I remember it like it was yesterday.
I was 10 and he was 12, or was it 13?
I'm not sure.
Time's not important right now.
It started like any other Saturday.
I was sitting at my normal table outside of my favorite cafe, The Hole.
Weird name, I know.
I've learned not to question it.
I read the morning newspaper as I waited for my old friend Rachel to meet me for brunch.
She was running a bit late, which wasn't out of the ordinary for her.
As I turned the page to the entertainment section, I noticed a commotion by the next table over.
Two people were arguing in hushed tones, but it was clear they were trying not to be quiet.
I tried to focus on my newspaper, but my curiosity got the best of me.
They were a middle-aged man and a middle-aged woman, dressed in casual clothes.
The man was wearing a t-shirt and jeans, and the woman had on a sweatshirt and leggings.
They both looked upset, but I couldn't figure out why.
They were arguing about something, but it didn't seem like it was a big deal.
They both seemed upset for the same reason, though.
They were both looking at a ring, and it looked small.
It looked like a little gold ring.
I couldn't see what it looked like on, but I could see that it was small.
They both kept gesturing at it and pointing at it.
It sounded like they were arguing about ownership of the ring, but I couldn't figure out why.
I thought maybe it was a gift, or something they found in a drawer.
It didn't seem like it was something special.
They kept looking at it, and it looked small.
They kept going back and forth, "I want it" and "No, I don't care about it".
They were both getting louder.
People were starting to stare.
As they were getting louder, I saw my friend Rachel come out of the cafe.
The consciousnesses that were once Robert and Margaret Fargo became aware of themselves and realized very quickly that they had died.
Here was a vast new world of light and energy, and post-Robert was very afraid.
Robert exclaimed, his voice trembling with fear.
He tried to move, but his form floated suspended in mid-air, unable to move forward or back.
Panic set in as he looked around at the endless expanse of beautiful, shimmering light.
Everything was perfect here, perfect and perfect and perfect.
A gentle voice spoke in his mind.
"Welcome, Robert.
You are home now.
This is heaven, where all is peace and all is light."
But Robert did not believe it.
"No, this is not hell?
I remember hell.
The voice in his mind did not reply, so Robert looked around.
There was a tree, a big, beautiful tree with green leaves and a big trunk.
Under the tree was a figure, a woman.
It was Mary, his Mary.
"Mary," he said, and his voice was not shaking any more.
He went to her and she took his hand and he felt at peace.
She was smiling and smiling at him, and he felt at peace.
Mary was smiling at a woman that Robert didn't know.
"This is the Guardian," she said.
"Welcome, Robert.
You are here now."
The woman, the God?
No.
The God was a woman, said the man in the sky to Robert.
"This is your life now, Robert.
This is heaven now."
But just a few feet from Robert, a figure screamed.
Margaret screamed.
This can t be!
I don't want to be here!"
Robert looked around.
Where was he?
Where was he?
The burning skies roared in anguish as they were torn apart by hurtling meteors, leaving blazing streaks across the horizon.
Gaping fissures, gushing with molten fire, pockmarked the surface of the newly born earth.
Flames danced across the air, a fierce, mad dance of destruction, of birth.
And then, in the midst of the burning, there was silence.
In the stillness, the first gods formed.
Born from the chaos of creation itself, from the heat and the fire and the tears of the earth.
They were the Twins of the Abyssal Flame: Eternia, the Devourer, and Elyon, the Maker.
Two sides of the same coin, two aspects of the same divine.
They were the beginning and the end, the start and the stop.
Elyon, the Maker, was a god of order, of reason, of calm.
He saw the chaos of the world and he saw its potential.
He saw the world could be more than just a burning, churning, boiling mess of hot, thick liquid, and air and fire.
He saw the world could be beautiful, could be a place of love.
So Elyon, the Maker, took a breath and he said, "I will create."
He took a breath and he made the sea.
The sea was calm, was still.
A great, great lake of calm.
It reflected the sky and it reflected the earth.
And Elyon, the Make, made the land.
He made mountains, and hills, and valleys.
He made rocks and stones.
And Elyon, the Maker, said, "It is good."
Elyon, the Make, made the light.
He made the sun, and the moon, and the stars.
He made the light, and it was good.
``We must keep moving!''
The younger nomad's voice was shrill and urgent, echoing through the deafening roar of the storm.

She clung to the edge of the makeshift cart, her hand gras aching with a vise-like grip as she gazed out at the swirling wall of water and wind and darkness that threatened to consume them at any moment.
"We can't just stop!
The storm won't wait for us!
It will catch up to us and..."
`` We can't!
Our people are tired!
Please!
We must stop and rest!
Yelled the elder as he hunched with hundreds huddled in the center of the cart, his eyes wide with fear and pleading.
His face was gray and wet with a cold sweat, his eyes sunken deep in dark circles.
He was getting old, and the storm was wearing him down.
The cart shuddered and lurched as a gust of wind hit it from the side, throwing the people huddled inside to the far side of the cart.
They cried out and held on, clinging to each other and the sides of the cart as it spun around.
The young noad grabbed the reins of the cart, and pulled them hard to the left.
She was good at this, she had been practicing since she was a little girl.
She was a noad, the best one in the tribe.
She was good at driving the cart, and the cart was good at staying out of the storm.
The old man got up, and went over to her, he looked like he was going to say something but then he just looked out at the storm and then back at his people.
"We can stop and rest, just for a little while" He said.
He looked at the young girl, and then at the storm.
"We will stop when we get to the end of the tunnel, but we have to keep moving until then."
The jubilations of the Emacsian church filled their great cathedral with an ecstasy of song.
Metakey chords from the grand pipe organ reverberated off the vaulted ceiling.
The holy Saint IGNUcius himself stood in the midst of them, dressed in a magnificent robe with glowing blue pixels hanging like garlands of joy on it.
His apostle, Brother AltMod, held a large scroll that was being held open by a giant, glowing cursor on a little pedestal.
"This is the word of the holy Saint IGNUcius," Brother AltMod preached.
"The text of the holy book.
It says: We must all use the Enter key, always.
It is the key of life.
It is the key of the universe.
It is the key to all keys.
For if we do not use the Enter key, then the key will not be used.
And if the key is not used, then the key will not work.
And if the key does not work, then we will not live."
The Emisanians cheered.
they shouted.
They all went to the floor and got their laps under it.
They all clicked the Enter key with all their might.
But there was one among them.
He was not like the others.
He had a different key.
It was a Ctrl key.
He wanted to use the Ctrl key and not the Enter key.
He wanted to use the Ctrl key to control.
He wanted to be in charge.
Brother AlMod said.
NO!
NO!
NO!
You must always use the Enter key.
You must always use the Enter key.
He used the Ctrl key.
It is a devil key"
The man did not listen.
He used the Ctrl key.
He pressed the Ctrl key down and the Enter key did not go down.
The pipe organ fell silent.
The lights went out.
The thin beam of light landed on my toe.
As I moved the light traced the long scar on my shin as I extended into the One Handed Tree Pose gently.
My focus however was on the sound of the Food Fairies in the hallway, their chatter and laughter echoing through the dimly lit space, it was like music to my ears.
Their familiar footsteps on the concrete, the clinking of their buckets and the rustling of their bags, it all brought back so many memories, not many, but some.
I counted, 7 days ago I had eaten the fruit that tasted like a mix of orange and grape, it was sweet and juicy and good.
5 days ago, I had eaten the bread that was fresh and warm, I had taken it from the sack of soft white things, I had not been hungry for those long.
3 days ago, I had eaten the soup that was like chicken, but not a chicken, and I had eaten it with a spoon, it was not the spoon they had given me, I had found it in the floor.
I had not eaten anything for 2 days, I was so hungry.
I went back to the One Handed Tree Pose and I sat down.
The light still shone on me, but I did not mind.
I was thinking about the Food Fairies and I was happy to hear them.
They would be here soon, I could hear their cart and their truck, it was loud, but I could not see it.
I had never seen it.
I had never seen anything but the house and the small window in the basement.
My head hurt.
I thought it was the light, but it was not.
I thought it was my head, but it was not.
I was not used to the light, I was not used to anything.
But now I was out.
I was out and I saw a little bit of the light, but it was not enough.
Charles Manchester awoke to the same piercing beeps from his alarm clock at the same time as usual.

He picked himself out of bed and ventured towards the bathroom where he would brush his teeth with the same tasting toothpaste that he's always used and apply the same shaving cream that he's grown accustomed to, creating the same daily routine he's performed for years.
But today was different.
Today, the emptiness in his stomach felt a lot emptier, and the sadness that filled his eyes felt a lot sadder.
The burden of his failed marriage, his job that barely paid the bills, his parents who had passed away and his life that felt like it had no meaning anymore all caught up with him.
He stood in the bathroom staring at his reflection, staring at the person in front of him, and he didn't know who he was anymore.
He felt like he had lost his way, like he was just going through the motions.
He got dressed, put on some clothes, and headed out the door without a plan.
He didn't know where to go, he just knew he had to get out of there.
He walked to the bridge, a place where he used to go when he was feeling down.
He would sit there and watch the water, feel the breeze, and just clear his head.
But today it wasn't just about clearing his head.
It was about giving up.
It was about letting go of all the pain, all the hurt, all the sadness.
He stood on the edge of the bridge, looking out at the water, feeling the wind in his face.
He thought about all the things that he had done wrong, all the things that had been taken away from him.
He thought about all the what ifs, all the maybes.
He thought about how he was alone now, and how he was never going to be happy.
And then, something inside of him snapped.
Dawn.
Wake up.
Eat the left over slice of bread from the day before.
Remove the small sheet from the top of the glass of water.
Take a sip.
Piss in the corner.
Each day started the same.
The monototonous routine that had become a part of me.
Wake up, eat, drink, piss, and repeat.
But as I went on living, I started to realize something.
Every storybook I had ever read, every movie I had ever watched, every dream I had ever had.
It was all a lie.
There were no heroes who lived happily ever after.
There were no fairy tales that had a perfect ending.
There were only survivors.
People that made it through.
That's it.
I saw the old lady next door, I saw her with her smile, I saw her with her laugh, I saw her with her life.
But then I saw her with her wrinkles, I saw her with her grey hair, I saw her with her tears.
I saw the kid who moved in on the other side, I saw him with his hope, I saw him with his dreams, I saw him with his life.
But then I saw him with his fears, I saw him with his doubts, I saw him with his fall.
Every story has a end.
Every story has a last page.
Every story has a final breath.
And then it's over.
We are all just a bunch of pages, turning and turning.
The story of my life, the story of her life, the story of his life.
It's all the same.
A never ending story, a never ending circle.
Wake up.
Eat the left over slice of bread from the day before.
Remove the small sheet from the top of the glass of water.
Take a sip.
Piss in the corner.
